hook: Ball or feather: which lands first?

explain.title: WHY?
lines: Air pushes back on the feather

source: NASA Space Power Facility · BBC Human Universe (2014)
caption: Bowling ball vs feather: which lands first? 🎳🪶 With air, the ball wins easily. Pump the air out and they land at the exact same time. What should we test next? 👇 #physics #science #gravity #vacuum #satisfying #nasa #3danimation
description: We drop a bowling ball and a feather side by side from 2 m inside a glass chamber. First with normal air inside, then after pumping the air out.

With air, the ball hits the floor after 0.64 s while the feather drifts down slowly: air pushes back on it, and for something so light and wide that push almost cancels its weight. On a bowling ball the same air resistance is tiny compared with its weight, so it falls almost freely.

In a vacuum there is no air to push back. Gravity gives every object the same acceleration, 9.81 m/s², whatever its mass, so both fall 2 m in 0.64 s and land together, both at about 6.3 m/s. NASA filmed exactly this in its Space Power Facility vacuum chamber for the BBC's Human Universe (2014), and astronaut David Scott did it on the Moon with a hammer and a falcon feather during Apollo 15 (1971).
The animation is a simulation. The vacuum drop follows t = √(2h/g). The feather's drift in air is illustrative only, which is why no time is shown for it in round 1.
sources_detail: NASA Glenn Space Power Facility (Plum Brook Station), world's largest vacuum chamber: bowling ball and feathers dropped together, filmed for BBC Two 'Human Universe' with Brian Cox (2014).
Apollo 15, 2 August 1971: David Scott drops a hammer and a falcon feather on the Moon; they land together (NASA NSSDC).
Free fall: t = √(2h/g) = √(2 × 2.0 / 9.81) = 0.639 s → shown as 0.64 s; impact speed v = g t = 6.26 m/s.
Simulated: 2 m drop, g = 9.81 m/s². In air the ball is treated as free fall; the feather's drift (slow terminal speed with sway) is illustrative, not measured.
